title: Restricting Hate Speech to Maintain Racial and Religious Harmony in Singapore
what_it_is: Restricting Hate Speech to Maintain Racial and Religious Harmony in Singapore

sections.label: Attacks and ISIS stronghold fall
sections.summary: A white man killed 50 Muslims in Christchurch mosques, a Turkish-origin man killed three in the Netherlands, and ISIS' last stronghold fell.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Eight days later on 15 March, a white man shot and killed 50 people – all Muslim – in two mosques in Christchurch.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Three days after that, on 18 March, a man of Turkish origin shot and killed three people in the Netherlands.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Five days after that, on 23 March, the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria's (ISIS') last stronghold fell.

sections.label: Ministry function on hate speech
sections.summary: The Ministry's core functions include dealing with hate speech to prevent conflict and violence among different races and maintain internal security.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Ensuring, among other things, that we deal with hate speech to prevent conflict, violence among people of different races so as to maintain internal security is one of my Ministry's core functions.

sections.label: Example of hate speech
sections.summary: A political leader calling members of a racial or religious group vermin that needs to be exterminated is an example of hate speech.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: An example of hate speech: political leader calling members of a racial, religious group "vermin" that "needs to be exterminated".

sections.label: Effects of repeated hate speech
sections.summary: Repeated hate speech increases people's prejudices, feelings of being threatened, and propensity to violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Repeated hate speech increases people's prejudices, feelings of being threatened, and propensity to violence.

sections.label: Normalising hate speech and early intervention
sections.summary: Neuro-imaging studies showed people are not thought of as social beings, and systematically developed hate speech makes discrimination and oppression socially acceptable, so civilisation must intervene early.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Neuro-imaging studies showed that you then do not think of these people as social beings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the lesson is that when hate speech is systematically developed, it becomes socially acceptable to discriminate and to oppress.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the important lesson is that civilisation must intervene early to prevent hate speech from becoming normalised.

sections.label: Studies and report on hate speech
sections.summary: Two PhD students' Warwick University study showed hate speech triggered hundreds of violent crimes against refugees in Germany, and Germany's 2015 report says uninhibited online hate speech can lead to radicalisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2018, two Doctorate of Philosophy (PhD) students did a study in Warwick University.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They showed that hate speech triggered hundreds of violent crimes against refugees in Germany.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Germany's Federal Ministry of the Interior's 2015 Annual Report says: "Uninhibited hate speech on the Internet can lead to individual or collective radicalisation." I am not going to read all of it.

sections.label: Skinhead music and violence
sections.summary: About 91% of terrorist skinheads limited music consumption to White Power bands, which the German government called the No 1 gateway to violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Approximately 91% of terrorist skinheads limited their music consumption to White Power bands.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The German government has described skinhead music as the No 1 gateway to violence.

sections.label: Malaysia Rebellion Fest cancelled
sections.summary: A music fest featuring Malay Power nationalists called Rebellion Fest was cancelled this month in Malaysia.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A music fest featuring Malay Power nationalists called Rebellion Fest, was cancelled just this month in Malaysia.

sections.label: Austrian courts convict Prophet critic
sections.summary: Austrian courts convicted a lady who had called the Prophet Muhammad a paedophile.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Austrian courts had convicted a lady who had called the Prophet Muhammad a paedophile.

sections.label: UK hate speech witnessed
sections.summary: In the UK religion can be ridiculed, and in 2018 more than a quarter of Britons witnessed hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But you can in the UK ridicule, insult, abuse any religion, beliefs, practices or the followers of such religions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, in the UK in 2018, more than one quarter of all Britons – that is more than 12 million people – witnessed hate speech.

sections.label: Christchurch manifesto banned
sections.summary: Attendees from the late 1990s to 2003 included Richard Reid, and after the Christchurch incident New Zealand's chief censor banned the shooter's manifesto.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: From the late 1990s to 2003, the attendees included Richard Reid, the shoe bomber for whom you can thank for having to take off your shoes each time you go past in an airport.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, in New Zealand, shortly after the Christchurch incident, New Zealand’s chief censor banned the shooter’s manifesto, "The Great Replacement".

sections.label: UN Secretary-General on hate speech
sections.summary: In February 2019 the UN Secretary-General called hate speech a menace and assigned a team to present a global plan of action.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the United Nations (UN) last month, February 2019, the UN Secretary-General called hate speech a "menace to democratic values, social stability, peace." He pointed out the dangers of allowing hate speech to move into the mainstream.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He said, "With each broken norm, the pillars of humanity are weakened." He has assigned a team to scale up the response to hate speech and present a global plan of action, on a fast-track basis.

sections.label: Race and religion survey
sections.summary: A 2016 CNA and IPS survey found race and religion play a large role in Singaporeans' personal decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you go to a 2016 survey by Channel NewsAsia (CNA) and the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS), race and religion play a large role in the personal decisions of Singaporeans.

sections.label: Prohibiting hate speech
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the House agrees hate speech in all forms is unacceptable and should continue to be prohibited and dealt with firmly.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They can be whipped up and, once blood has been shed, the years of nation-building we have done will come to naught.” The experience of other countries shows when you are clear, you have firm laws prohibiting hate speech, you deal fairly with all communities, then you can start building a multiracial, multi-religious, harmonious society.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I hope there will be agreement in this House that hate speech, whatever form it takes – religious, political, entertainment – in all its different forms, is unacceptable and we should continue to prohibit hate speech and deal with it firmly, in the way we have done so far.

sections.label: Restrictions on offensive speech
sections.summary: The environment will be conducive for discrimination and eventually violence, which is why there are restrictions on offensive speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The environment will be conducive for discrimination, eventually violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is why we have restrictions on offensive speech, even when it is, strictly speaking, not hate speech.

sections.label: Offensive material cases
sections.summary: In 2009 a couple was charged over offensive material on the Prophet and Islam, and Nicholas Lim and Benjamin Koh made offensive postings.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2009, a couple was charged for distributing highly offensive material on the Prophet, on Islam, and they sent it to Muslims.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Nicholas Lim, a young man, he made a post by reference to Malays, in response to a letter in the Straits Times' Forum page, "Can cabs carry uncaged pets?" Benjamin Koh, he made a posting, "Muslims are pigs.

sections.label: Legal framework on offensive speech
sections.summary: The position is that offensive speech should generally not be allowed in public discourse, with the legal framework set out in the Penal Code, Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and Sedition Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Our position so far has been very practical and nuanced.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We take the view that offensive speech should generally not be allowed in public discourse.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And the current legal framework – I am not going to go into it – but the Penal Code, sections 298, 298A; the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, section 8; the Sedition Act, sections 3 and 4; set out the legal framework.

sections.label: Offensive speech on race and religion
sections.summary: The speaker clarifies he is speaking about offensive speech in relation to race and religion, in the context of preserving harmony and preventing unrest and violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In this context, let me make one point clear again.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I am speaking about offensive speech in relation to race, religion and in the context of preserving racial, religious harmony, preventing unrest, violence.

sections.label: MHA and offensive speech
sections.summary: MHA deals narrowly with preventing violence and security aspects of offensive speech aimed at racial and religious divides.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) deals, more narrowly, with prevention of violence, the security aspects arising from offensive speech and directed at racial and religious divides.

sections.label: Impact of speech context
sections.summary: The likely impact of speech has more salience if said from the pulpit or at an election rally.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What is the likely impact of the speech?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It has more salience, for example, if said from the pulpit or at an election rally.

sections.label: Speaker, context, occasion, reach
sections.summary: Impact differs by who says it, the context, occasion, nature of event, and reach, such as 50 people privately versus publicising generally.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The impact, therefore, will be different, depending on who says it and the context.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We also consider the occasion, the nature of the event, and the reach: there is a difference between saying it to 50 people in a private setting compared with publicising it generally.

sections.label: Pragmatic approach versus absolute approach
sections.summary: The Government says both absolute approaches are not doable and undesirable, making its pragmatic approach the only tenable one.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Members will see that either absolute approach is really not doable.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, I think Members will probably agree with me that the absolute approach is undesirable, so that brings up back to the pragmatic approach that the Government takes as the only tenable one for our society.

sections.label: Western traditions and foreign preachers
sections.summary: Singapore is not as liberal as many Western societies, and in 2017 two foreign Christian preachers were rejected after one called Allah a false god.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Here, the context of what is acceptable in Western traditions is relevant.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We are not as liberal as many Western societies and our approach differs.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But we have allowed some books, movies, performances and concerts even though a variety of different religious groups have found them objectionable.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In doing that, we assess the reaction of our community, whether there are immediate security issues or longer-term security issues, by building in deeper fault lines, or whether we think that even though they are unhappy, this is not going to contribute to deepening of fault lines.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If Members look at our approach to foreign preachers, in 2017, the Ministry of Manpower, in consultation with MHA, rejected the applications of two foreign Christian preachers to speak in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: One of them had described Allah as "a false god" and various other things.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Very charismatic and powerful but that is why we banned him.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Segregationist, divisive, he said "we should not greet someone else".

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, we have HDB flats, we live next to one another.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Muslim does not greet the Christian and the Christian does not greet the Muslim.

sections.label: IPS study on religious leaders
sections.summary: The 2019 IPS Study shows 82% of people believe a religious leader should not influence votes in elections.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The 2019 IPS Study shows that 82% of our people believe that a religious leader should not be influencing people's votes in elections.

sections.label: Imam Nalla supplication, Work Pass
sections.summary: In 2017, Imam Nalla recited a supplication calling for victory over Jews and Christians at Friday prayers and was asked to leave Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2017, a preacher in a local mosque, Imam Nalla, recited a supplication that called for God to grant victory – some people said it is help – over Jews and Christians during Friday congregational prayers.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: He was on Work Pass and was asked to leave Singapore.

sections.label: Pastor Rony Tan insulting beliefs
sections.summary: In 2010, Christian pastor Rony Tan insulted, trivialised and ridiculed Buddhist and Taoist beliefs in a video that was uploaded.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In 2010, we had a Christian pastor insulting, trivialising, ridiculing the beliefs of Buddhists and Taoists, a gentleman by the name of Rony Tan recorded on video and uploaded.

sections.label: Bilahari Kausikan double standards response
sections.summary: Mr Bilahari Kausikan responded and pointed out double standards protecting Jews while standing by vilification of Islam in the name of free speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Mr Bilahari Kausikan responded and pointed out the double standards to protect one group – the Jews – while standing by the vilification of another religion – Islam – in the name of free speech.

sections.label: Protection from hate speech
sections.summary: The state will strive in every way possible to achieve racial and religious harmony, protecting people from hate speech and unacceptable offensive speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: You and members of your faith will be protected from hate speech, unacceptable offensive speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The state will strive in every way possible to achieve racial, religious harmony.

sections.label: Tolerance of hate speech
sections.summary: Tolerance of hate speech does not breed tolerance of difference.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Tolerance of hate speech does not breed tolerance of difference.

sections.label: Race discussion openness survey
sections.summary: Two-thirds felt discussions on race were disconcerting because they could be offensive and lead to tension, showing fault lines remain and run deep.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Openness to race discussion – two-thirds felt that discussions on race was disconcerting because it could be offensive and lead to tension.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, Members can see we have done well, but the fault lines remain and they run deep and they can be exploited.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: When two-thirds of Singaporeans believe that merely talking about racial issues causes tension, what do you think about offensive speech?

sections.label: Concert licence restrictions imposed
sections.summary: The concert would be R18 with songs removed, no religious symbols, no religion in dialogue, and no denigration of faith or violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The restrictions were quite substantive: the concert would be classified Restricted 18 (R18); removal of songs that may be potentially sensitive; no religious symbols used during the concert; no reference to religion in the band's on-stage dialogue; content should not denigrate any faith or promote any cult practices, nor advocate or promote violence in any way; no ritualistic or satanic acts; and a number of other conditions.

sections.label: MHA asks IMDA to cancel
sections.summary: On 7 March MHA asked IMDA to consider cancelling the concert, and IMDA cancelled the licence two days later over MHA's concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On 7 March, MHA asked IMDA to consider cancelling the concert, that is, two days later, and IMDA cancelled the licence in view of MHA's serious concerns.

sections.label: MHA advised IMDA to cancel
sections.summary: Because many Christians felt the concert was deeply offensive and denigrating, MHA advised IMDA to cancel, a decision the speaker made.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Given that many Christians felt this was deeply offensive and denigrating, MHA advised IMDA to cancel.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It was my decision that MHA should so advise IMDA.

sections.label: REACH survey on cancellation
sections.summary: A REACH survey found 60% were aware of the cancellation; of those, 86% of Christians and 64% overall agreed with it.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Our assessment of public sentiment turned out to be correct, because a subsequent feedback unit Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH) survey showed that, first of all, that 60% were aware of the cancellation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Of those who were aware, 86% of Christians agreed with the cancellation.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But 64% of all who had heard about the cancellation, Christian and non-Christian, also agreed with the cancellation.

sections.label: Government responsibility on Watain licence
sections.summary: The issue is whether Government should license Watain publicly, and it has a responsibility to offended Singaporeans, not just music fans.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The issue here is about whether the Government should give Watain licence to perform publicly in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And the Government has a responsibility to not just the individuals who like the music, but also the majority of Singaporeans who would be offended.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If we allowed this concert, we would have to allow other such concerts.

sections.label: 2013 IPS Survey findings
sections.summary: The 2013 IPS Survey found most Malays, Chinese, Indians, Muslims, Christians and Catholics rated race or religion important to identity, and most backed police reports for insults.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In the 2013 IPS Survey, 95% of Malays said race was important to identity.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Eighty-five percent of Chinese and Indians said the same; 97% of Muslims said religion was important for identity; 91.4% of Christians said that and 89.5% of Catholics said the same.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Eighty-five percent of the respondents said that a Police report should be made when someone pokes fun at racial, religious groups; 87% of the respondents said a report should be made when someone insults another racial or religious group in a public setting; 86% of respondents said a report should be made when there is material criticising other religions or racial beliefs.

sections.label: Survey on religious leader comments
sections.summary: 97% said a religious leader should not make insensitive comments about another's religion, and 95% said they should not discourage mixing with other religions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Ninety-seven percent said that a religious leader should not make insensitive comments about another’s religion and 95% said a religious leader should not encourage his followers not to mix with members of another religion.

sections.label: No influence and preacher bans
sections.summary: The speaker says no one, Christian or otherwise, influenced him, and that he decided to ban two Christian preachers in 2017.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: No one – Christian or otherwise – influenced me.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I also decided to ban two Christian preachers in 2017.

sections.label: Government action on hate speech
sections.summary: The Government will be fair, even-handed and practical, but will not hesitate to act on hate speech and offensive speech that deeply wounds communities.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But the Government will be fair, even-handed and has to be practical.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But I reiterate – where hate speech is concerned, where offensive speech is concerned, where vast numbers of any community find it deeply wounding, we will not hesitate to take action.

sections.label: Internet outages and anti-immigrant violence
sections.summary: The study found that when Facebook had Internet outages or service disruptions, anti-immigrant violence dipped in places where it was high.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What was telling about that study is that when there were Internet outages or service disruptions to Facebook, incidence of anti-immigrant violence dipped in the very places where they were high.

sections.label: Video views before takedown
sections.summary: The video was viewed 4,000 times before it was taken down.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The video was viewed 4,000 times before it was taken down.

sections.label: Bill on deliberate online falsehoods
sections.summary: The Bill tabled on Deliberate Online Falsehoods is one step.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Bill that has been tabled on Deliberate Online Falsehoods is one step.

sections.label: Singapore tolerance of ethnic minorities
sections.summary: A 2016 Gallup World Poll ranked Singapore top of 140 countries for tolerance of ethnic minorities, with 96% respecting people of all races.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: In a Gallup World Poll in 2016, Singapore ranked top out of 140 countries for tolerance of ethnic minorities.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Ninety-six percent agreed or strongly agreed with the statement “I have respect for people from all races”.

sections.label: Ethnic quotas in housing
sections.summary: The passage states ethnic quotas were imposed in housing to prevent racial enclaves and possible ghettoes in housing estates.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: People accuse us of "social engineering". "So what?" I ask.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We imposed ethnic quotas in housing to prevent racial enclaves in our housing estates and possible ghettoes – banlieus, as they are called in France.

sections.label: Multiracial determination at independence
sections.summary: The founding Prime Minister said Singapore was not a Chinese, Malay or Indian nation, and the Government based its legitimacy on appealing to all Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On the very first day of our existence as a sovereign, independent state, the founding Prime Minister said, "This is not a Chinese nation, not a Malay nation, not an Indian nation." From the beginning, the Government determined it will base its legitimacy by appealing to all Singaporeans, not just the majority Chinese.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That determination to be multiracial, multi-religious; that determination that no one will be squatted upon on account of his race or religion, the colour of his skin or the language he speaks, that is why we became independent and we mean to keep it that way.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If anything, we are prepared to err on the side of caution and risk over-reacting to preserve harmony, rather than take chances and risk explosions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, reflecting back in a New York Times interview, said in 2010, "I’ve got to tell the next generation, please do not take for granted what’s been built.

sections.label: Singapore's multiracial meritocracy values
sections.summary: The passage states Singapore is 54 years old, a multiracial meritocracy, and its values are not yet so deeply embedded to be unassailable.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: What we have in Singapore is precious, hard fought.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But we are only 54 years old, a multiracial meritocracy, unique, but the values are not yet so deeply embedded to be unassailable.

sections.label: Lives lost to senseless violence
sections.summary: The passage states at least 50 people lost their lives to senseless violence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: At least 50 people lost their lives to senseless violence.

sections.label: Deaths and homes destroyed
sections.summary: The passage states that in one day more than 50 people lost their lives and 186 homes were destroyed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In one day, more than 50 people lost their lives and 186 homes were destroyed.

sections.label: Casualties killed and wounded
sections.summary: Over 100 were wounded and at least 20 were killed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Over 100 were wounded and at least 20 were killed.

sections.label: Constitution protects race and religion
sections.summary: Article 12 of the Constitution provides unique protection to race and religion within Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Indeed, Article 12 of our Constitution provides unique protection to race and religion within Singapore.

sections.label: Respectful differing views not hate speech
sections.summary: A respectful, logical, evidence-backed differing view for Singapore's good cannot be taken as hate speech, and the law codifies the correct standard.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Therefore, when someone presents a differing view in a respectful, logical and cogently reasoned manner, with evidence to back up their position, with an eye for the good of Singapore, that cannot be taken as hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Therefore, in my view, the law as it currently stands ensures and codifies the correct standard.

sections.label: Section 298 and Amos Yee case
sections.summary: Section 298 of the Penal Code was among the charges in Public Prosecutor v Amos Yee Pang Sang, where the conviction was upheld on appeal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Section 298 of the Penal Code was one of the criminal charges in question in Public Prosecutor v Amos Yee Pang Sang.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Section 298 reads: "Whoever, with deliberate intention of wounding the religious or racial feelings of any person, utters any word or makes any sound in the hearing of that person, or makes any gesture in the sight of that person, or places any object in the sight of that person, shall be punished." The District Judge in that case found that Yee's "comments about Jesus, the central figure of Christianity, are clearly derogatory and offensive to Christians." On appeal to the High Court, the conviction was upheld and the judgment stated that the methodology in the language "has been to use coarse and hard-hitting words to arouse emotions", "using vulgarities and insults to deliberately provoke the reader and to draw him out, in the words mentioned in the charge".

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: It is also because of robust pieces of legislation, such as section 298 of the Penal Code, that I fully supported Minister Shanmugam's intervention in the Watain saga and the eventual banning of the Watain concert.

sections.label: Banning Ashley Madison and Watain
sections.summary: MSF banned the Ashley Madison portal to protect family values and public morality, and the Government was correct to cancel Watain's performance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Just as how the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) stepped in to ban the Ashley Madison extramarital dating portal to protect our family values and public morality, the Government was correct to cancel Watain’s performance.

sections.label: Home Team and ISD trust
sections.summary: The environment of trust depends on organisations such as the Home Team and the ISD preventing fractious disharmony in society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Would we have that environment of trust if we did not have organisations, such as the Home Team and the ISD, constantly tilling the soil to prevent fractious disharmony in our society?

sections.label: Terrorist attacks by far right
sections.summary: The speaker says many people were surprised that over 70% of terrorist attacks are carried out by far right, non-Muslim, often white attackers, a fact the Minister shared.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A fair number of people I spoke to were surprised that more than 70% of all terrorist attacks are carried out by far right, non-Muslim and often white attackers, a fact Minister shared during his recent speech to the Religious Rehabilitation Group.

sections.label: Sedition Act offensive speech cases
sections.summary: The MHA annex covered 14 incidents from 2005 to 2017 invoking the Sedition Act and Penal Code, none in performing arts, 11 online.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The annex to the MHA statement covered 14 incidents from 2005 to 2017 where the Government had to invoke the Sedition Act and Penal Code to deal with offensive speech, including the issuance of stern warnings and conditional warnings against various individuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: None of these interventions involved offensive speech in the performing arts or entertainment space.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Unsurprisingly, however, 11 out of the 14 cases involved comments made online, on Facebook, on blogs or in online chatrooms.

sections.label: IPS survey on young people
sections.summary: An IPS survey found young people take a more permissive attitude to offensive speech, though this does not necessarily mean they approve of it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Separately, a recent IPS survey observed that young people take a more permissive attitude to offensive speech, a fact which does not necessarily suggest that they approve of it, but they are prepared for a discussion on such issues.

sections.label: IMDA conditions for Watain concert
sections.summary: IMDA's conditions allowed Watain to perform with offensive songs removed, no religious references or symbols, no ritualistic acts, R18 rating and maximum 200 attendees.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: By its own admission, IMDA's conditions in originally allowing Watain to perform in Singapore included the removal of songs which were religiously offensive, the band could not make references to religion or use religious symbols and that no ritualistic acts like showering the audience in pig’s blood as had been done before in another jurisdiction, were to be performed on stage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Furthermore, given the band's history and concerns expressed by MHA, IMDA allowed the Watain concert with a rating of Restricted 18 (R18) and on the condition that it would be a very small concert with only a maximum of 200 people allowed to attend.

sections.label: Petition and concert cancellation
sections.summary: Two days before the performance, an online petition sought to ban Watain and Soilwork, and MHA requested IMDA cancel the concert on the day itself.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Two days before the band’s slated performance, a widely publicised online petition made its rounds seeking to, I quote "ban satanic music groups Watain and Soilwork from performing in Singapore." MHA thereafter requested IMDA to cancel the concert on the day of the scheduled performance and at the eleventh hour.

sections.label: IMDA letter on cancellation
sections.summary: IMDA's letter to The Straits Times Forum said the cancellation was due to new and serious concerns about public order and social and religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: According to IMDA's letter to The Straits Times Forum, the cancellation of the concert was due to new and serious concerns about public order, and ground reactions relating to social and religious harmony.

sections.label: Watain promoters compensation question
sections.summary: It asks which agency will compensate Watain's promoters and what amount the wasted expenditure comes to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Separately, which agency will compensate Watain’s promoters and what amount does the wasted expenditure come up to?

sections.label: Secular society and religious harmony approach
sections.summary: It supports the Government's secular and religious harmony approach, urging care, a graduated approach over bans, education and the Golden Rule.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Overall, the Government’s careful and balanced approach to uphold a strictly secular society so as to preserve a common public space, and its principles towards religious harmony as enunciated in the 1989 White Paper on the Maintenance of Religious Harmony and, separately, the latest MHA statement in 2017 are sound and should be supported.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But the Government must be careful not to be perceived as taking sides but instead err on the side of wisdom, especially on matters that are expressions of free speech, particularly in the entertainment and performing arts space.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Instead of a hard policy, such as bans, a graduated approach establishing a range of conditions like that done by IMDA in its original assessment of the Watain concert may better reflect the compromises required to create and sustain as accommodating and robust a common public space as possible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A robust education system which continues beyond school – one that enjoins Singaporeans to ascribe to an attitude of live and let live, respect for both the religious and non-religious, and dealing with fellow citizens with tolerance and mutual respect, with the knowledge that we only have one another to lean on in good times and bad, are equally, or if not more important.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Ultimately, it is the Golden Rule – that we should not do unto others as we would not have others done to us – that must be the dictum all Singaporeans, be it in the online or real world.

sections.label: Platform antagonism on social media
sections.summary: It states digital infrastructures let hate spread, and describes platform antagonism as using fake identities to discredit ethnic, cultural or religious groups.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Digital information infrastructures, including social media, such as Facebook, and participatory media, such as Reddit, allow hate to propagate in innovative and insidious ways.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The first is an alarming practice termed as platform antagonism.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This refers to the use of fake identities in social media platforms to discredit particular ethnic, cultural or religious groups.

sections.label: Racist views as dark humour
sections.summary: It states a second concern is disguising racist and nationalist views as dark humour on participatory media.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: A second issue of concern is disguising racist and nationalist views as dark humour on participatory media.

sections.label: Online hate speech spreading swiftly
sections.summary: It states that online hate speech, emboldened by anonymity, interactivity and mass connectivity, can sweep through communities swiftly and insidiously if unchecked.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Emboldened by anonymity, fuelled by interactivity and powered by mass connectivity, online hate speech can sweep through communities swiftly and insidiously if left unchecked.

sections.label: Tim Berners Lee on hate speech
sections.summary: It cites Sir Tim Berners Lee saying free speech is great but hate speech is not, and that today's information infrastructures make hate speech hard to contain.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Indeed, the inventor of the World Wide Web, Sir Tim Berners Lee, alluded to the fact that his creation is still in its awkward teen years.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: He declared that, I quote, "when you grow up, you have to accept responsibility, you have to realise that free speech is great but hate speech is not." As it stands, today's information infrastructures make it difficult to contain hate speech.

sections.label: Christchurch attack and online hate speech
sections.summary: The Christchurch terror attack shows the Internet lets people spread harmful hate speech, so society must change the online environment.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   The terror attack at Christchurch tells us that the Internet, being a communication medium, presents certain problems.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: It can allow people harbouring hatred to freely produce and spread hate speech which is harmful to the society.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Our society must act to change the online environment to prevent the harmful effects of hate speech and online falsehoods.

sections.label: Overhauling information infrastructures
sections.summary: More must be done to overhaul information infrastructures so hate speech and online disinformation are minimised, and incentive structures and revenue models recalibrated.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: (In English): Mr Speaker, a great deal more must be done to overhaul our information infrastructures so that hate speech and online disinformation are minimised, if not obliterated.

sentences.speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Incentive structures and revenue models must be recalibrated to make the online environment more positive and edifying.

sections.label: Impact of hate versus offensive speech
sections.summary: Research shows hate speech and offensive speech have no difference in impact, only taking more time for offensive speech to influence humans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Research also shows that there is no difference in the impact of hate speech as opposed to offensive speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It only takes more time for humans to be similarly influenced with respect of offensive speech.

sections.label: Notice issued in Hindi
sections.summary: A market operator recently issued a notice in Hindi instead of the Tamil language.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Recently, a market operator issued a notice in Hindi instead of the Tamil language.

sections.label: Tamil as official language
sections.summary: Minister Iswaran had assured that the Tamil language is one of Singapore's four official languages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Minister Iswaran had assured that the Tamil language is one of four official languages of Singapore.

sections.label: Interfaith support and online falsehoods report
sections.summary: Taoist temple organisations helped Muslims at Hari Raya Haji prayers, and the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods made 22 recommendations on weaponising social media.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For example, during the Hari Raya Haji prayers last year, two of our Taoist temple organisations built a tent at Bukit Batok Central for the benefit of around 1,000 Muslims so that they can perform their Hari Raya prayers led by an Ustaz from the Ar-Raudhah Mosque.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We are truly fortunate to have far-sighted religious leaders like Dr Suhami and his peers from the various religions in Bukit Batok.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: We must continue to strengthen interracial and inter-religious relations so that hate speech, which can potentially divide our different races and religions, will not take root in our society, in order to safeguard Singapore's cohesiveness and solidarity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: On the phenomenon of weaponising social media, this has been dealt with in depth in the report of the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods which made 22 recommendations, and I would not say more on this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I do think, however, that there is a need to see how we can prevent or deprive any commercial entity or person from making money by being platforms or providing support for hate and offensive speeches that may create disaffection along racial and religious lines.

sections.label: Rethink ousting judicial review
sections.summary: The speaker suggests reconsidering the decision to oust judicial review of Government action under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and the Internal Security Act for hate speech incidents affecting racial and religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Next, I suggest a rethink on the decision to oust judicial review of Government action under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and the Internal Security Act to deal with hate speech incidents that affect the maintenance of racial and religious harmony.

sections.label: Judicial review assurance and signalling
sections.summary: Judicial review by the independent Judiciary provides assurance and signalling to concerned people, with its narrow focus being legality, rationality and procedural propriety of Executive decisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Judicial review by the Judiciary, which is an independent branch of our Government, will provide an important assurance and signalling effect to people having such concerns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This does not mean that the judiciary will substitute its decision on the matter; the narrow focus of judicial review is to ascertain the legality, rationality and procedural propriety of the Executive’s decision.

sections.label: MCCY BRIDGE dialogues and youth conversations
sections.summary: AMA is an initiative under MCCY's BRIDGE providing safe spaces for dialogue, with over 200 at a Catholicism session and over 8,000 youths in Youth Conversations, and a 2019 panel.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: AMA is one of the initiatives under the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth's (MCCY's) Broadening Religious and Racial Interaction through Dialogue and General Education (BRIDGE), which provides safe spaces for such honest and open dialogues to take place.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Over 200 people turned up at one recent session on Catholicism in December 2018 to learn more from members of the Catholic Archdiocese.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Beyond religious issues, MCCY’s Youth Conversations have allowed more than 8,000 youths to come together and share perspectives on issues of national importance, such as social divides, vulnerable communities and environmental sustainability.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: In 2019, a panel will be formed to further engage youths.

sections.label: International Conference on Cohesive Societies
sections.summary: Singapore will continue learning internationally about social harmony and will hold the International Conference on Cohesive Societies in June, bringing together policymakers, leaders and academics.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We will also continue to learn from experiences and best practices internationally about promoting and preserving social harmony.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We will be holding the International Conference on Cohesive Societies in June this year, where we will bring together policymakers, community and religious leaders and academics from Singapore, the region and the wider world to share experiences, discuss ideas and promote collaboration.

sections.label: Museums, heritage and hawker culture
sections.summary: Museums and heritage institutions foster understanding of diverse cultural heritage anchored on shared history, and national pride is expressed in the UNESCO bid for hawker culture.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Our museums and heritage institutions foster deeper understanding of our diverse cultural heritage anchored on our shared history.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We express our national pride in the rich diversity of our hawker culture in our ongoing United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) bid.

sections.label: Sport and youth participation
sections.summary: Sport brings people together, and more opportunities will be provided for children and youth to play through ActiveSG Clubs and Academies, with expanded Outward Bound Singapore participation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Sport is an activity that brings people from all walks of life together.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We will strive to provide children and youth with more opportunities to play with one another from a young age, through the ActiveSG Clubs and Academies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We have also expanded participation in Outward Bound Singapore (OBS).

sections.label: Expanding SG Cares Community Networks
sections.summary: The SG Cares Community Networks are being expanded to connect volunteers and resources to areas of need.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: For instance, we are expanding the SG Cares Community Networks to better connect volunteers and other resources to areas of need.

sections.label: Constitution and laws protect communities
sections.summary: The Constitution and laws protect different communities' interests, including prohibiting hate speech and behaviour inciting violence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Our Constitution and laws protect the interests of different communities, including the prohibition of hate speech and behaviour that incite violence.

sections.label: Building mutual trust among Singaporeans
sections.summary: Moving from tolerance to mutual trust requires constant effort from Government and people, with Singaporeans reaching out and listening to one another.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: This is the process of moving from tolerance, accommodation and celebrating our diversity to mutual trust.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: It requires constant effort from both the Government and the people.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Singapore's long-term peace and stability require Singaporeans to reach out and listen to one another, communicate and build mutual trust, one encounter at a time.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Singapore is a home for all of us, bound by friendship and a common destiny.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Let us uphold the principle of safeguarding cultural and religious diversity, march towards the goal of a united nation, regardless of race, language and religion, and write a unique, exciting chapter of our Singapore Story.

sections.label: Existing laws sufficient against hate speech
sections.summary: The Penal Code, Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and Sedition Act are sufficient to deter offensive and hate speech, and the Watain concert licence was validly revoked.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I am glad to know that this is not so.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I think the current legal framework standing in sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code, the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, and sections 3 and 4 of the Sedition Act is sufficient to deter offensive and hate speeches.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I believe it is important for the Minister to reiterate and to confirm that this Statement is merely to establish clarity of the current provisions and approach and that no one, no Singaporean, needs to be alarmed that there are additional measures or safeguards against hate and offensive speech that threatens our harmony here.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: One is the right of choice for people to choose; second is the freedom of expression; the third is, I guess, the reluctance of the state to be perceived as overly paternalistic and also the reality, the tactical reality, that the concert was already given the go-ahead by IMDA and cancellation would cause inconvenience to and displeasure of the organisers and the attendees.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: However, as more information was uncovered on the group, it became clear that revoking the concert licence to perform was a valid move and there are good reasons for this.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: The Watain leader's confirmation that he totally encourages, I quote, "any kind of terrorist acts committed in the name of Watain" runs counter to what SG Secure is trying to promote.

sections.label: Support for revoking Watain concert permission
sections.summary: The speaker supports revoking the Watain concert permission and hopes lessons are learnt on due diligence and stakeholder consultations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: They, too, voiced their support for the cancellation, as confirmed in a recent Berita Harian report.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: It is unfortunate that, in this instance, the Government's decision was reversed so close to the event date, just a couple of days, even when it affects a small group.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: But for the Government to go ahead with the concert just because it was initially approved, after knowing what it now knows or uncovered, would have been a wrong decision.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: I, therefore, support the Minister's decision to revoke permission for the Watain concert to carry on and I hope we have learnt valuable lessons from it in the areas of better due diligence and also earlier consultations with key stakeholder groups so that future episodes can be managed more effectively.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: First, on how the public will know or is educated on what constitutes acceptable, offensive and hate speech and, second, on how the Government is going to enforce the current framework to reach a healthy and not an unhealthy state of restraint.

sections.label: Understanding acceptable speech without fear
sections.summary: The passage asks how understanding can be achieved with typical Singaporeans without causing unnecessary fear or unhealthy self-censorship.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: In this framework of "it depends" guided by "commonsense", how can an understanding be achieved with the typical Singaporean, with the man in the street, so as not to cast any unnecessary fear or any unhealthy self-censorship in society?

sections.label: Enforcing restrictions on hate speech
sections.summary: A speaker asks how the Government will enforce restrictions on hate speech, citing survey findings on acceptance of extremist views.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: If policymakers are serious about restricting hate and offensive speech to defend our racial and religious harmony that we so value, how does the Government plan to enforce this approach?

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: There ought to be a clearer and publicised process by which violations are reported, for instance, and decisions by the Government to be consulted with the relevant stakeholder groups, such as key religious and non-key religious groups or leaders.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: And just because an approach may be hard to implement does not mean that we cannot learn to implement it or apply it better.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: So, notwithstanding my request for clarifications, Sir, I totally and strongly support the Ministerial Statement.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Of the 1,800 Singapore residents interviewed, one in four found it acceptable for religious extremists to publish their views on the Internet or social media.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: A significantly higher proportion of younger people found the publication of extreme views acceptable, with almost half of those surveyed aged 18 to 25 saying they would allow such publication.

sections.label: Watain ban on religious harmony grounds
sections.summary: MHA recommended Watain not perform in Singapore on religious harmony grounds, with no value judgement on black metal music.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: In other cases, it could touch significantly on the sensitivities of other groups in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: So, on religious harmony grounds, MHA recommended that Watain not be allowed to perform in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: In the ban on Watain, there is no value judgement on black metal music.

sections.label: Early judgement calls on performances
sections.summary: Judgement calls on whether music and performances harm racial and religious harmony should be made as early as possible.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Thirdly, while a judgement call has to be made on whether music and performances harm racial and religious harmony, such judgement calls should take place as early as possible so as to minimise confusion to arts practitioners and misunderstanding from the public that the Government makes decisions based on pressure from religious groups.

sections.label: Christchurch attack and online hate speech
sections.summary: A gunman killed 51 Muslims praying in a mosque, saying online hate speech incited his racial discrimination and violence.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   At the recent terrorist attack in Christchurch, the gunman killed 51 Muslims who were praying in the mosque.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: According to the gunman, it is the online hate speech and contents that have incited his racial discrimination and violent behaviour towards the Muslims.

sections.label: Laws against racial and religious enmity
sections.summary: Singapore's laws strictly forbid words and actions that instigate racial and religious enmity.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: Our laws strictly forbid words and actions that instigate racial and religious enmity.

sections.label: Violence against Chinese in Indonesia
sections.summary: In 1998 Black May riots and 1965 ethnic cleansing in Indonesia, many Chinese were killed and women raped.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: For example, in 1998, during Indonesia’s Black May riot which targeted the Chinese community, there were almost 1,000 Chinese killed and nearly 500 Chinese women raped in Jakarta alone.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs and National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
sentences.text: During the 1965 ethnic cleansing in Indonesia, about 50,000 Chinese were slaughtered.

sections.label: Content licensing and creative expression
sections.summary: A speaker suggests licensing agencies coordinate better and communicate decisions earlier, while warning against reducing space for creative expression.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One, as someone leading an arts company that presents concerts here and overseas, I would like to make a suggestion that the agencies responsible for licensing content coordinate better.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Decisions made must be communicated earlier, so that show organisers can make the necessary plans without incurring unnecessary expenses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Two, while we make sure that we regulate hate speech and protect our social fabric, we also need to make sure that we do not end up reducing the space for creative expression and imagination.

sections.label: Performance licences and agency consultation
sections.summary: Agencies should study and consult professionals before granting performance licences, and clarify what is allowed to avoid last-minute cancellations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Before performance licences are granted, agencies must do in-depth studies and consult professional opinions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We must work together to avoid last-minute cancellations because this will lead to mistrust in the relevant agency and people will question its authority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I hope the relevant agencies can make it clear what is allowed and what is prohibited, so that more arts companies can have a better understanding and take proactive measures when planning their future performances.

sections.label: Christchurch mosque attack reaction
sections.summary: The speaker says the Christchurch mosque attack seemed distant but was shocked to find it was not that distant.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The recent attack on two mosques in Christchurch, the event may seem distant but, indeed, I was shocked when I found out it was not that distant after all.

sections.label: Late Tariq among Christchurch victims
sections.summary: The late Tariq was one of many innocent lives lost among the 50 who died in Christchurch.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The late Tariq was one of many innocent lives lost among the 50 who died in Christchurch.

sections.label: Laws protecting social harmony
sections.summary: Policies and laws exist to root out behaviours threatening social harmony, including the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, Penal Code sections and the Sedition Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Indeed, we have many policies and laws in place to root out behaviours and factors that threaten social harmony, such as the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and Penal Code sections 298, 298A, 267C and 505, and also the Sedition Act.

sections.label: Agreement on hate speech approach
sections.summary: The speaker agrees with the Minister that logic and reasoning are likely ineffective against hate speech and supports Singapore's middle-ground approach to offensive speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I wish to state my views early on in my speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I fully agree with the Minister and the facts and studies he shared that addressing hate speech targeting ethnic, religious communities via logic and reasoning is likely to be ineffective.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Normalising it and allowing it to proliferate are dangerous.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I also agree with the Minister that restrictions on offensive speech, even when it is strictly speaking not hate speech, needs to be applied judiciously and I still think Singapore's current approach in dealing with offensive speech via the assessment of words and the material and its likely impact on the targeted community is a middle-ground approach to take, relative to a blanket ban on all offensive speech and material.

sections.label: IPS study on hate speech
sections.summary: An IPS study found many aged 18 to 25 would allow such views if they do not instigate harm, and an inter-Ministry approach is hoped for.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Many of them, according to the IPS study, are aged 18 to 25 who indicated they would allow such views to be espoused as long as these do not instigate harm on others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: My earlier story with regard to my resident highlighted the dangers, the deadly dangers, of hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: So, I hope we would initiate an inter-Ministry approach, involving MHA, MCCY, the Ministry of Education and MCI to look into this.

sections.label: Religious harmony efforts expansion
sections.summary: The Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and Penal Code sections largely self-censor comments, and efforts should expand beyond school to the workplace and community.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Because we have the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and the relevant Penal Code sections, these comments are already largely self-censored, so imagine what hateful words would transpire if we did not have the Act in place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The Government should expand efforts to encourage racial harmony beyond school to the workplace, as well as working with the community.

sections.label: Programmes for young parents
sections.summary: Young parents should be exposed to programmes promoting opportunities to mingle with people of all races and religions and experience their culture.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: As such, I would like to suggest that young parents be exposed to programmes that will promote opportunities for them to mingle with people from all races and religion, and to experience their culture.

sections.label: Religious institutions as starting places
sections.summary: Religious institutions with large networks of beneficiaries and NGOs are good places to start if they accept volunteers of any religion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Religious institutions, with their large network of beneficiaries and non-governmental organisations (NGOs), are good places to start, if they open themselves to accepting volunteers of any religion.

sections.label: Hate speech glorification not allowed
sections.summary: Anything that seeks to glorify hate speech must not be allowed in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: As long as it is something that seeks to glorify hate speech, it must not be allowed in Singapore.

sections.label: Corporate partners and labour unions
sections.summary: Work with corporate partners and labour unions to educate employers and employees to reduce perpetuating stereotypes or build whistleblowing policy on discrimination and stereotyping actions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Can we also work with our corporate partners and labour unions to educate our employers and employees to reduce efforts to perpetuate stereotypes or build whistleblowing policy on discrimination and actions that stereotype certain segments?

sections.label: Children's Internet access and hate speech
sections.summary: Children as young as eight have Internet access, and the speaker looks forward to laws reining in those who spread hate speech online.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: In Singapore, children as young as eight years old have access to the Internet.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: This is a crucial matter that we have to pay attention to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I look forward to the strengthening of our laws to rein in those who spread hate speech via Internet platforms and social media.

sections.label: Hate speech consequences and public education
sections.summary: Hate speech should not be tolerated and its propagators must face consequences, while public education and community trust build immunity against it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: Hate speech should not be tolerated and those who propagate it must be made to face consequences, including punishment to serve as deterrent.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: To borrow medical terminology, we need to build our herd or group immunity against hate speech through the vaccine of public education and of building trust among communities to overcome ignorance and misinformation.

sections.label: Watain music group example
sections.summary: The music group Watain is cited as one such example.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The music group, Watain, is one such example.

sections.label: Calibrated approach to offensive speech
sections.summary: The speaker says hatred advocates cannot have it both ways and supports a calibrated approach to offensive speech that may injure racial and religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: People who advocate hatred, chaos and destruction cannot have it both ways.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: We must protect and nurture this precious but delicate asset to the best of our ability.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: We should never take it for granted but seek, instead, to constantly fortify and strengthen it.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I support the broad principle that we should have a calibrated approach to address offensive speech that may injure racial and religious harmony.

sections.label: State must reject religious policy attempts
sections.summary: The state must address, manage and even reject attempts by religious and ethnic groups to advance public policy based on their own versions of truth.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: If we each seek to dye the water according to our own particular persuasion, we will soon find that there is nothing but darkness there.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Therefore, the state must directly address, manage, and even reject, when necessary attempts are made by religious and ethnic groups to advance public policy based on their own versions of the truth.

sections.label: Risk of religiously shaped public sphere
sections.summary: Advocating public policy on shared religious interests or common offence risks normalising that religiously or racially held interests can shape the public sphere.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To advocate public policy on the basis of shared religious interests, or a common feeling of offence across groups, risks normalising a dangerous principle, that religiously or racially held interests can shape the public sphere.

sections.label: IPS religion survey findings
sections.summary: An IPS report found nearly two in three Christians, Catholics and Muslims would follow religious principles over conflicting secular law.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In the 2019 "Religion in Singapore: The Private and Public Spheres" IPS report, Mathews, Lim and Selvarajan found that nearly two in three Christians, Catholics and Muslims claimed they would follow religious principles over a conflicting secular law.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Moreover, a substantial minority of Christians, Catholics and Muslims believe it is acceptable for religious leaders to speak on changes to the law which are in conflict with religious principles.

sections.label: Offence, intent and law
sections.summary: The passage argues offence cannot be left to community views and that intent must be considered alongside offence.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, the question of offence cannot simply be left to community views, given the strict laws we have in place.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In a multi-religious and racial society, this may lead to the "weaponisation" of the law against other communities and the public space, as Prof Cherian George has argued.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Second, intent must be considered together with the question of offence.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: When the intention is to honestly criticise or to promote an alternative social or religious principle that conflicts with entrenched interests, this is the contest of ideas at work, and we suppress it at our own peril.

sections.label: Enlightened secularism for public space
sections.summary: It states that otherwise the public space would be ceded as each community shapes it, so enlightened secularism must be promoted.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To do otherwise would be to cede the public space slowly over time as each community uses their power to shape the public space in accordance with their own way of life.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We must promote an enlightened secularism to protect the public space in the interests of all.

sections.label: Middle way and Christchurch attack
sections.summary: It advocates a middle way, neither too tight nor too loose, and cites the Christchurch mosque attack that killed 50.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, best is to take the middle way, not too tight and not too loose.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There is an old saying tie your camel before it goes astray." About two weeks ago, we all read in shock about the news of a 28-year-old Australian, radicalised by Islamophobic material online, who attacked two mosques in Christchurch, killing 50 and injuring many others.

sections.label: Survey on extremists and Muslims
sections.summary: The survey found one in four respondents accepted religious extremists publishing views, higher among younger Singaporeans, and 15% found Muslims threatening.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The survey found that one in four respondents had no qualms about letting religious extremists publish their views online or hold public meetings to talk about them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This number was much higher, close to 50%, amongst younger Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Around 15% of respondents also found Muslims at least somewhat threatening.

sections.label: Fifteen percent statistical significance
sections.summary: It states that 15% is statistically significant and roughly the size of Singapore's Malay/Muslim population.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Fifteen percent is statistically significant, and is, in fact, roughly the size of our entire Malay/Muslim population in Singapore.

sections.label: Youth wing in IRCCs
sections.summary: The passage suggests considering a youth wing in all IRCCs in Singapore to lead such initiatives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, there is value in considering having a youth wing in all IRCCs in Singapore, which can take the lead in spearheading such initiatives.

sections.label: Civil society tech collaboration
sections.summary: The passage calls for greater collaboration between civil society, non-profit organisations and tech companies like Facebook, Twitter and Google.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, I would like to call for greater collaboration and partnership between civil society and non-profit organisations with tech companies, such as Facebook, Twitter and Google, to trial innovative community-based solutions.

sections.label: World Interfaith Harmony Week adoption
sections.summary: The passage recommends adopting the World Interfaith Harmony Week in Singapore, noting the UN adopted it on 20 October 2010.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Thirdly, although we have Racial Harmony Day, to place greater emphasis on the importance of religious harmony in Singapore, I would like to recommend the adoption of the World Interfaith Harmony Week in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Just under a month later, on 20 October 2010, it was unanimously adopted by the UN and, henceforth, the first week of February will be observed as a World Interfaith Harmony Week.

sections.label: Public Service leading as employer
sections.summary: The passage suggests the Public Service, as Singapore's largest employer, can take the lead in this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As the largest employer in Singapore, perhaps the Public Service can take the lead in this.

sections.label: Understanding other cultures for harmony
