sections.summary: The passage states understanding other racial and religious groups' cultures promotes harmony, especially among youths, and benefits households and the country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In addition to understanding one’s own cultural pride and glory, it is also very important for everyone to also understand clearly the culture of other racial and religious groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In particular, our youths having the right understanding of all races will promote harmony amongst us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Understanding culture correctly will enhance family and social ties, thereby benefiting every household and the country.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For us to interact and communicate together with the people of a multiracial society, an understanding of one another’s culture will provide great assurance.

sections.label: Singaporeans accepting religious extremist views
sections.summary: The passage notes a sizeable number of Singaporeans accept religious extremists publishing views or holding public meetings, with about four in 10 younger people aged 18 to 25 finding publishing acceptable.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Researchers noted that a sizeable number of Singaporeans have no qualms about allowing religious extremists to publish their views online or hold public meetings to talk about them.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Roughly four in 10 younger people aged between 18 and 25 felt that publishing was acceptable, possibly because of this group's increasingly liberal attitudes towards free speech.

sections.label: Need for legislation
sections.summary: The speaker holds that legislation is needed to draw a line setting out what is criminal and unacceptable to society.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: My personal view is that we need to have legislation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: We cannot do without drawing a line that sets out what is criminal, what is unacceptable to a society.

sections.label: Offensive expressions assessed in context
sections.summary: The speaker says an exhaustive definition of offensive expressions is impossible and accepts the Government's framework of assessing context, impact and mainstream community views.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I think it would be impossible to set out an exhaustive definition of offensive expressions, and we would probably have to look at each case in context.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I, therefore, accept and agree with the Government’s current framework of assessing in material the context and the impact to the particular community towards which the harm may be caused and, in particular, to benchmark it to the mainstream views within the community.

sections.label: Survey on Muslims as threats
sections.summary: Over 70% of Singaporeans feel different faiths can get along, but some 15% find Muslims threatening, with private-housing residents more likely to think so.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: More than 70% of Singaporeans feel that people of different faiths can get along when living close together, but some 15% find Muslims threatening.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: Researchers found that those who dwell in private housing were more likely to think that Muslims are threats, compared with those who dwell in HDB flats.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: IPS senior research fellow Dr Mathew Mathews said, "There is little question that global terror and how it has often been associated with Muslims has fed into the minds of a small group of Singaporeans, who thus feel that Muslims are threatening." It is a solemn reality that Muslims here in Singapore must face.

sections.label: Support for Government restrictions
sections.summary: The speaker is grateful for a Government that speaks out against Islamophobia and supports its restrictions to maintain racial and religious harmony.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I am truly grateful for a Government that speaks out against Islamophobia even before it became fashionable to do so and continues to take the effort to protect interests of all in the community, including the minority groups.

sentences.speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
sentences.text: I am, therefore, supportive of the Government’s efforts in putting appropriate restrictions to maintain racial and religious harmony in Singapore.

sections.label: Riots fuelled by hate speech
sections.summary: The speaker later learned someone they knew had been killed in riots fuelled by hate speech among people of different races and religions.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I would then later learn that somebody whom they knew had been killed in the riots.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: These racial conflicts were fuelled by hate speech among people of different races and religions.

sections.label: Firm stand against hate speech
sections.summary: The speaker states that preserving harmony requires taking a firm stand against hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: To preserve harmony, we need to take a firm stand against hate speech.

sections.label: Impartial hate speech law enforcement
sections.summary: The law must be applied impartially to protect all racial and religious groups, and hate speech should be reported.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: When restricting hate speech, we must apply the law impartially to protect all racial and religious groups.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Certain groups might even start to suspect the Government, which will undermine our society and security.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I urge anyone who hears of hate speech against your community, to make a report.

sections.label: Government tapping goodwill ambassadors
sections.summary: The Government should tap on this group to be ambassadors of goodwill on the ground.

sentences.speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Government should tap on this group to be ambassadors of goodwill on the ground.

sections.label: British press and Muhammad caricatures
sections.summary: In 2015 the British press collectively decided not to republish the caricatures of Prophet Muhammad that led to the Charlie Hebdo killings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In 2015, the British press, unlike some newspapers in Europe, collectively decided not to republish the caricatures of Prophet Muhammad which led to the slaughter of 12 staff working in the office of Charlie Hebdo.

sections.label: UK hate speech offence laws
sections.summary: UK laws make it an offence to use threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour causing harassment, alarm or distress.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In the UK, laws make it an offence for a person to use "threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour that causes, or is likely to cause, another person harassment, alarm or distress".

sections.label: Germany online hate speech law
sections.summary: Germany's 2017 law fines social media companies for failing to remove hate speech, and deletion rates varied by platform.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Standing against this, our existing laws may be good enough as there are adequate provisions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, I argue that what we need is tighter and proactive enforcement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: In 2017, Germany became the first country in the EU to introduce a dedicated law against online hate speech that allows authorities to fine social media companies which fail to remove hate speech posts that violate German law within 24 hours.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: Companies could be fined up to €50 million under the law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: This came about after the German government examined a report showing a 77% surge in hate crimes in Germany in the previous year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: As an immediate response to the law, in January and February 2017, Youtube deleted 90% of hate speech videos reported by users, Twitter deleted 1%, Facebook deleted 39%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, laws have effect, but not all the time.

sections.label: Australia political culture tolerating hate speech
sections.summary: Politicians in Australia blamed the New Zealand tragedy on immigration and got away scot-free due to a tolerant political culture.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: We have seen politicians there saying that the real cause of the New Zealand street tragedy to be "the immigration programme that allowed Muslim fanatics to migrate to New Zealand in the first place" and these politicians have gotten away scot-free.

sentences.speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
sentences.text: So, this is not because Australia does not have laws against hate speech, although some may argue that such laws have been weakened in recent years, but it is because there is a political culture there that tolerates such open airing of views.

sections.label: Ban on hate speech
sections.summary: Singapore firmly bans hate speech in any form and medium, unlike countries allowing it under free speech, to prevent exploitation of social fault lines.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: For this reason, I am glad that our approach to the increasing prevalence of hate speech has been a firm ban against it, in any form, in any medium.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Whilst other countries may allow it in the name of freedom of speech, here, we recognise the very real and severe implications that hate speech can have.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Such an approach has helped to prevent fault lines in our society from being exploited by individuals or groups with extremist agendas.

sections.label: Regulating music and entertainment
sections.summary: Singaporeans may access entertainment, but music undermining social and cultural stability is untenable, so regulation is crucial to prevent hate.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Whilst Singaporeans have the freedom to access various forms of entertainment, music that undermines our social and cultural stability is untenable.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Hence, the regulation of music and entertainment is crucial to preventing the spread of hate.

sections.label: IPS Survey on Muslims
sections.summary: A recent IPS Survey found 15% of respondents found Muslims threatening, meaning Singapore's multi-religious fabric remains vulnerable to hate speech.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: A recent IPS Survey showed that 15% of respondents found Muslims threatening.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: This means that Singapore’s multi-religious fabric is still vulnerable to the threat of hate speech.

sections.label: Protection for minorities
sections.summary: The Government's stand would give minorities confidence they are protected from hate, their culture preserved, and religions practised peacefully, with community leaders urged to preserve the social compact.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: Our Government's stand would give all minorities the confidence that they would be protected from the target of hate, their culture would be preserved and they can practise their religions peacefully.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: All of us, as minorities, should play our part, too.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministers for Education and Minister for Social and Family Development (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
sentences.text: I call upon our community leaders to lead and steward the community to be appreciative of how precious our social compact is and be active to preserve.

sections.label: Members on hate speech
sections.summary: Members agree hate speech impacts racial and religious harmony, requires early and decisive intervention, and offensive speech needs restrictions.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Hate speech impacts racial and religious harmony and Members agree generally that, in dealing with hate speech, we have to intervene early and decisively.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: On offensive speech that may not be considered hate speech, Members agree that we need to have restrictions.

sections.label: No change in frameworks
sections.summary: There is no change in IMDA's content regulation framework, which has worked well, and no change in MHA's approach.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The Member asked about future applications in general.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is no change in IMDA’s framework on content regulation – it has worked very well so far.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: They have had to apply it and they have applied it in all these years.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: There is also no change in MHA's approach to these issues.

sections.label: Restricting hate and offensive speech
sections.summary: The Member is said not to disagree that hate speech cannot be allowed and offensive speech must be restricted.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Equally, I do not think the Member disagrees that we cannot allow hate speech and we must restrict offensive speech.

sections.label: Risks from hate speech
sections.summary: The speaker outlines risks of hate and offensive speech, and accepts a risk of religion influencing or narrowing public policy space.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And that might then affect the secularity of the government, not in the French sense, but in the sense that this Government is secular.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, if we were to look at today's debate, I outlined one big risk in my opening speech which can arise from hate speech and offensive speech, the fault lines, the kind of violence that can arise from it and the deep splits between communities and religions, or religious groups.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira hinted at another big risk – which is not within the frame of today's debate but I accept it as a risk – of religion either trying to influence public policy or narrowing public policy space.

sections.label: Strong fair political leadership
sections.summary: The answer given is that strong political leadership fair among the different religions is needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The answer is that you really need a strong political leadership which is fair among the different religions.

sections.label: Hate speech and terrorism response
sections.summary: The speaker says terrorism has no colour, race or religion, urges dealing with hate and offensive speech, and notes the Motion lapses.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Last week’s event has proven as evidence to the entire world that terrorism has no colour, has no race and has no religion." We need to step forward on hate speech.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We need to deal decisively with offensive speech so that someone will not have to make this eulogy in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: But if it happens, I hope that we will be able to respond in the same way that the New Zealanders have done.

sentences.speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
sentences.text: Pursuant to Standing Order 44(2), the Motion to consider the Ministerial Statement on Restricting Hate Speech to Maintain Racial and Religious Harmony in Singapore lapses at the conclusion of debate.
